mainTopic: How to read and place the word הללויה, who first said הלל, and how joy relates to the שכינה and to Torah study
overview: The משנה ends with saying הללויה, so the גמרא first asks whether words ending in יה, like הללויה, ידידיה and מרחביה, are one word or two. רבי יוחנן, רב and רבה give different lists, and רב's own statements show he splits ידידיה and הללויה, treating the יה as a holy name. רבי יהושע בן לוי reads הללויה as one word ('many praises'), but elsewhere he seems to contradict himself. The גמרא then asks who first said הלל: שמואל says the נביאים set it up, רבי מאיר says דוד wrote all of תהלים, and רבי יוסי argues that הלל goes back to the sea. Along the way it explains words in תהלים and teaches that the שכינה rests only through שמחה של מצוה. It then settles how a teacher can be joyful while a student must sit in awe. A ברייתא lists six historical moments when הלל was first sung, and the חכמים say the נביאים set it for every trouble and every redemption. The amud ends by debating whether a border הללויה ends one chapter or opens the next, and begins comparing this to the משנה and a ברייתא about where בית שמאי and בית הלל stop הלל. That comparison continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: הללויה, כסיה, and ידידיה are each one word
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא quotes רבי יוחנן: הללויה, כסיה, and ידידיה are each a single word.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: the words הללויה, כסיה, and ידידיה are each one word.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the word הללויה from the משנה. רבי יוחנן rules that three words ending in יה are each one single word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some words in תנ"ך end with the letters יה, which can be a name of ה׳. Calling a word 'אחת הן' means it is treated as one unit and not split into two words. Many מפרשים explain that this also means the ending יה is not treated as a separate holy name.

keyTerms.meaning: A word from שמות 17:16 (כי יד על כס יה)
Yedidyah, a name given to שלמה המלך (שמואל ב 12:25)
They are one, meaning each is a single word

steps.confusionAlert: 'אחת הן' does NOT mean the three words are the same as each other. It means that EACH of these words is one single word rather than two.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
"Halleluyah" and "Kesyah" and "Yedidyah"
are one (each is a single word).
phrases.notes: Each word is one unit and is not divided into two.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion of the word הללויה mentioned in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יוחנן, הללויה, כסיה, and ידידיה are each one word.

steps.title: רב: כסיה and מרחביה are each one word
steps.stepSummary: רב gives a different list: כסיה and מרחביה are single words.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: כסיה and מרחביה are each one word.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion is brought. רב agrees about כסיה but adds מרחביה, and he does not mention הללויה or ידידיה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's list only partly overlaps with רבי יוחנן's list. Both include כסיה. רב adds מרחביה (from תהלים 118:5, ענני במרחב יה), and he leaves out the other two words. This gap is the reason the גמרא later asks what רב holds about ידידיה and הללויה.

phrases.english: Rav said: "Kesyah" and "Merchavyah"
are one (each is a single word).

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, differing opinion on which words count as one word.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רב, כסיה and מרחביה are each one word.

steps.title: רבה: Only מרחביה is one word
steps.stepSummary: רבה holds that only מרחביה is a single word. All the others are two words.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: only מרחביה is one word.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion is given. רבה narrows the list down to just one word, מרחביה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבה's view, even כסיה is two words. So in כסיה, הללויה, and ידידיה, the יה is its own separate word. מרחביה is the only exception, because there the ending expresses greatness ('a great expanse').
steps.whatToRemember: There are three views. רבי יוחנן: הללויה, כסיה, ידידיה are one word. רב: כסיה and מרחביה are one word. רבה: only מרחביה is one word.

phrases.english: Rabbah said: only "Merchavyah" (is one word).

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third, narrowest opinion in the same dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבה, only מרחביה is one word. All others are two words.

steps.title: What does רב חסדא hold about מרחביה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב חסדא (citing רבי יוחנן) treats מרחביה, since it was not on his list.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: according to רב חסדא, what is the status of מרחב יה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question about a word that רב חסדא did not mention. It wants to know whether he would count מרחביה as one word or two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא's list did not include מרחביה, but רב and רבה both treat it as one word. Leaving it out could mean he holds it is two words, or it could mean he simply did not mention it. Notice that the word is written here as two words (מרחב יה), which shows exactly what is being asked.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked (an open question raised in the בית מדרש)

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
"Merchav-yah" according to Rav Chisda, what is it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a word missing from the first opinion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רב חסדא treat מרחביה as one word or two?

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: No answer is found, so the question about מרחביה according to רב חסדא remains open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand (unresolved).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot find a source to answer the question, so it closes it with תיקו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means the question stays undecided. We do not know whether רב חסדא considers מרחביה one word or two.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question remains unresolved

phrases.english: Let it stand (unresolved).

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּיקוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question from step 4 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב חסדא's view on מרחביה remains undecided.

steps.title: What does רב hold about ידידיה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רב treats ידידיה as one word or two, since he did not list it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: according to רב, what is the status of ידידיה?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins about a word that רב left off his list. The next step will bring an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said ידידיה is one word, but רב did not mention it. The גמרא wants to know whether רב's silence means he disagrees.

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
"Yedidyah" according to Rav, what is it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question, this time about רב's opinion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רב treat ידידיה as one word or two?

steps.title: רב explicitly says ידידיה is two words
steps.stepSummary: רב himself said ידידיה is split into two words: ידיד is ordinary, and יה is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רב said: ידידיה is divided into two. Therefore 'ידיד' is ordinary and 'יה' is holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting another statement of רב. That statement shows he treats ידידיה as two words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since ידידיה is two words, the part ידיד is a regular word (חול). The ending יה is a holy name of ה׳‎ (קודש) and must be treated with respect, like other names of ה׳. This also shows that רב disagrees with רבי יוחנן about ידידיה.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: introduces a source that answers the question

steps.whyThisMatters: Whether a word is split decides whether its יה ending is a holy name. That affects how the word is written and treated, for example whether it may be erased.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rav said:
"Yedidyah" is divided into two;
therefore: "yedid" is ordinary, "yah" is holy.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 6 with an explicit statement of רב.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב holds ידידיה is two words: ידיד is ordinary and יה is holy.

steps.title: What does רב hold about הללויה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רב treats הללויה as one word or two.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: according to רב, what is the status of הללויה?
steps.whatsHappening: Another question begins about a word missing from רב's list, this time הללויה. The next step brings the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the word from the משנה itself. רבי יוחנן said it is one word, and רב did not mention it. So the גמרא asks what רב holds.

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
"Halleluyah" according to Rav, what is it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel question to step 6, about a different word.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רב treat הללויה as one word or two?

steps.title: רב saw הללויה split across two lines in a ספר תהלים
steps.stepSummary: רב reports that he saw a ספר תהלים in his uncle's house (רבי חייא) with הללו on one side and יה on the other. This shows it is two words.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, for רב said: I saw a ספר תהלים in the house of my uncle, in which 'הללו' was written on one side and 'יה' on the other side.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with רב's eyewitness report about how הללויה was written in a ספר תהלים. It was split into two parts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A single word may not be split across two lines. Since the ספר wrote הללו at the end of one line and יה at the start of the next, הללויה must be two words. So רב disagrees with רבי יוחנן here as well.

keyTerms.meaning: The house of my uncle (רבי חייא, רב's uncle)
Side (here, one line or edge versus the next)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, both ידידיה and הללויה are two words, and the יה in them is holy. רב חסדא's view on מרחביה stays unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rav said:
I saw a book of Tehillim of the house of my uncle
phrases.notes: חביבא refers to רבי חייא, רב's uncle.

phrases.english: in which "Hallelu" was written on one side,
phrases.notes: That is, at the end of a line.

phrases.english: and "Yah" on the other side.
phrases.notes: That is, at the start of the next line, so the word was split.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַב: חֲזֵינָא תִּילֵּי דְּבֵי חַבִּיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 8 using רב's report of a written ספר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב holds הללויה is two words, as shown by a ספר תהלים that split it across lines.
steps.raayaObject: That הללויה is two words according to רב
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's eyewitness account of the ספר תהלים in רבי חייא's house

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי reads הללויה as one word
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבי יהושע בן לוי disagrees with רב. He reads הללויה as one word meaning 'praise Him with many praises.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And this argues with רבי יהושע בן לוי, because רבי יהושע בן לוי said: What does 'הללויה' mean? Praise Him with many praises.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רב's view (הללויה is two words) is not the only view. רבי יהושע בן לוי reads it as one word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, the 'יה' at the end is God's holy name. For רבי יהושע בן לוי, 'יה' just makes the praise bigger, like saying 'lots of praise.' So in his view, the ending is not a name of God at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And this disagrees (with someone else's view)
Halleluyah: the word whose reading is being discussed

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי יהושע בן לוי is against praising God. He agrees הללויה is praise. He only argues about whether the ending 'יה' is God's name or a word that makes the praise stronger.
steps.whyThisMatters: If 'יה' is not a holy name, there is no problem writing or erasing it the way one would worry about a שם. That is why the one-word versus two-word question matters.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi,
phrases.notes: 'This' means רב's view that הללויה is two words.

phrases.english: for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
What does 'Halleluyah' mean?
Praise Him with many praises.
phrases.notes: Here 'יה' makes the praise stronger. It is not God's name.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְלִיגָא דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that רב's two-word reading, proven in step 9, is disputed by another אמורא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהושע בן לוי, הללויה is one word meaning 'praise Him with many praises.' The 'יה' is not a divine name.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי seems to contradict himself
steps.stepSummary: Elsewhere, רבי יהושע בן לוי lists ten kinds of praise in תהלים. He calls הללויה the greatest because it holds God's name and praise together. That treats הללויה as two words, which goes against his own view in step 10.
steps.simpleTranslation: And his own words argue with his own words, because רבי יהושע בן לוי said: ספר תהלים was said with ten kinds of praise: ניצוח, ניגון, משכיל, מזמור, שיר, אשרי, תהלה, תפלה, הודאה, and הללויה. The greatest of all of them is הללויה, because it includes God's name and praise at the same time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבי יהושע בן לוי said two things that do not fit together. Here he says הללויה contains God's name, which means two words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 10, the 'יה' was only a word that adds strength, not a name. Here he says הללויה is the greatest praise because it contains a שם ('יה') and praise ('הללו'). These two statements clash, and the גמרא simply notes this without solving it.

keyTerms.meaning: His own words disagree with his own words (he contradicts himself)
God's name and praise together at one time

phrases.english: And his own statement disagrees with his own statement,
for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
With ten expressions of praise
the book of Psalms was said:
With 'nitzuach,' with 'niggun,' with 'maskil,'
with 'mizmor,' with 'shir,' with 'ashrei,'
with 'tehillah,' with 'tefillah,' with 'hodaah,' with 'Halleluyah.'
The greatest of them all is 'Halleluyah,'
because it includes God's name and praise at one time.
phrases.notes: This means 'יה' is God's name, which matches the two-word reading.

steps.triggerLanguage: ופְלִיגָא דִּידֵיהּ אַדִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets רבי יהושע בן לוי's statement in step 10 against another statement he made.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע בן לוי's one-word reading of הללויה in step 10
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He also says הללויה contains a שם and praise. That only works if 'יה' is God's name, meaning two words.
steps.whatToRemember: On הללויה: רב reads two words (הללו + the שם יה). רבי יהושע בן לוי reads one word ('many praises') in one place, but elsewhere says it contains God's name, so he contradicts himself.

steps.title: משה and Israel sang שירת הים
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes שמואל: the song written in the תורה (שירת הים) was said by משה and the Jewish people when they came up out of the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: The song in the תורה was said by משה and the Jewish people at the time they came up from the sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: who first said the songs of praise. This first line sets up the next question about הלל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל starts with the clear case: שירת הים was said by משה and the Jews right at the sea. This gives a starting point, so the next question can ask who first said הלל.

keyTerms.meaning: The song in the Torah: the Song at the Sea (שירת הים)
At the time they came up from the sea

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
The song in the Torah,
Moshe and the Jewish people said it
at the time they came up from the sea.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how to read הללויה to who first said the songs of praise.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שירת הים was said by משה and the Jewish people when they came up from the sea.

steps.title: Who said הלל?
steps.stepSummary: Continuing שמואל's teaching, the question is asked: who first said this הלל?
steps.simpleTranslation: And this הלל, who said it?
steps.whatsHappening: A short question that sets up the next step: who first said the הלל from the משנה (תהלים chapters 113 to 118)?
steps.deeperAnalysis: We know who said שירת הים, but הלל is not part of that story. So the question is who first said it and why the Jewish people say it.

keyTerms.meaning: Hallel: the praise chapters (תהלים 113 to 118) said on special days

phrases.english: And this Hallel, who said it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַלֵּל זֶה מִי אֲמָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After naming who said שירת הים, it asks the same question about הלל.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who first set up or said הלל, and when it is said.

steps.title: The נביאים set up הלל for Israel
steps.stepSummary: The נביאים among the Jewish people set up הלל. It is said on special occasions, in times of trouble (praying the trouble will not come), and in thanks when the people are saved.
steps.simpleTranslation: The נביאים among them set it up for the Jewish people, so they would say it on every special occasion, and over every trouble, that it should not come upon them. And when they are saved, they say it about their being saved.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer: the נביאים set up הלל. It also tells us the three kinds of times the Jewish people say it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הלל has three uses: special times, times of danger, and times of rescue. It was not a one-time song like שירת הים. It was set up to be said again and again.

keyTerms.meaning: They established (set up as a practice)

steps.confusionAlert: 'שלא תבא עליהן' is a polite way of speaking: 'every trouble, may it not come upon them.' It does not mean we say הלל only when there is no trouble. We say it to pray against trouble.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why הלל is a set תקנה that we say on many occasions, including the סדר, and not just a song from one moment in history.

phrases.english: The prophets among them established it for the Jewish people
that they should say it
on every single special occasion,
and over every single trouble
(may it not come upon them).
And when they are redeemed,
they say it over their redemption.

steps.triggerLanguage: נְבִיאִים שֶׁבֵּינֵיהֶן תִּקְּנוּ לָהֶן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The נביאים set up הלל, to be said on special occasions, in times of trouble, and when the people are saved.
steps.whatToRemember: שירת הים was said by משה and the Jewish people at the sea. הלל was set up by the נביאים to be said again and again: on special days, against trouble, and in thanks for being saved.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: דוד said all the praises in תהלים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי מאיר: every praise in ספר תהלים was said by דוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי מאיר used to say: All the praises said in ספר תהלים were all said by דוד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with רבי מאיר's view on who wrote the praises of תהלים: all of them come from דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a new opinion on who wrote the songs. Since הלל is part of תהלים, רבי מאיר's view would make דוד its author. That sits differently from the idea in step 14 that the נביאים set it up.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Meir used to say:
All the praises stated in the book of Psalms
all of them were said by David,

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, הָיָה רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another source on who wrote the praises of תהלים, after step 14 said who set up הלל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every praise in ספר תהלים was said by דוד.

steps.title: The פסוק read as 'all these are דוד's prayers'
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר proves his view from the פסוק 'כלו תפלות דוד בן ישי.' He reads 'כלו' (are finished) as 'כל אלו' (all these).
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'כלו (ended are) the prayers of דוד son of ישי.' Do not read it 'כלו'; instead read it 'כל אלו' (all these).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר shows where his view comes from. He uses a new reading of a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The simple meaning of the פסוק is 'the prayers of דוד are finished.' By reading 'כלו' as 'כל אלו,' it becomes 'all these are the prayers of דוד.' So the whole book is דוד's.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introducing a פסוק)
Do not read it as (a teaching based on a new reading of the words)

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תיקרי' does not mean the text of the פסוק is changed. It is a way of learning an extra lesson from how the words could sound. The written word stays the same.

phrases.english: As it is stated: 'Ended are the prayers of David son of Yishai' (Psalms 72:20).
Do not read 'kalu' (ended),
but rather 'kol elu' (all of these).
phrases.notes: Read this way, the פסוק says all these prayers are דוד's.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״כׇּלּוּ תְפִלּוֹת דָּוִד בֶּן יִשָׁי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for רבי מאיר's view in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: רבי מאיר's claim that דוד said all the praises in תהלים
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים 72:20, 'כלו תפלות דוד בן ישי,' read as 'כל אלו.'
steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר says דוד said all of ספר תהלים. His proof reads 'כלו' as 'כל אלו': 'all these are the prayers of דוד.'

steps.title: Who said this הלל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who first said הלל, according to the view that does not agree with רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: This הלל, who said it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question to set up the next discussion: who was the first to say הלל? The answer comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר just said that דוד said every praise in תהלים. This question looks at the specific chapters of הלל and asks whether they really started with דוד or are older.

keyTerms.meaning: The set of praise chapters (תהלים קי״ג–קי״ח) said on holidays

phrases.english: This Hallel, who said it?
phrases.notes: A setup question for the opinions that follow.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַלֵּל זֶה מִי אֲמָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from רבי מאיר's claim that דוד said all of תהלים.

steps.title: אלעזר: משה and ישראל said it at the sea
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי quotes his son אלעזר, who says that משה and ישראל said הלל when they came up out of the sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: my son אלעזר says that משה and ישראל said it when they came up from the sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The first answer is given: הלל goes back all the way to the time of קריעת ים סוף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this view, הלל is much older than דוד. דוד may have later written it into ספר תהלים, but the song itself was first said by משה and ישראל at the sea.

keyTerms.meaning: My son אלעזר (רבי יוסי speaking about his son)
When they came up out of the sea

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
My son Elazar says:
Moses and Israel said it
at the time they came up from the sea.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר, אֶלְעָזָר בְּנִי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: משה and ישראל said הלל at the sea.

steps.title: The colleagues: דוד said it
steps.stepSummary: אלעזר's colleagues disagree with him and say that דוד said הלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: His colleagues disagree with him and say that דוד said it.
steps.whatsHappening: A second, opposing opinion is given: הלל was first said by דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This view matches רבי מאיר's idea that דוד is the author of the praises in תהלים. Now there is a clear מחלוקת: the time of the sea versus the time of דוד.

phrases.english: And his colleagues disagree with him,
saying that David said it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲלוּקִין עָלָיו חֲבֵירָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the opposing view to אלעזר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד was the first to say הלל.

steps.title: רבי יוסי sides with his son
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says that his son אלעזר's words seem more correct than the colleagues' words.
steps.simpleTranslation: And his words seem more correct than their words.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי decides which view he prefers: his son's view, that הלל goes back to the sea. This sets up the two proofs that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a short ruling of preference, not yet the reason. The next two steps explain why אלעזר's view makes more sense.

phrases.english: And his words appear more correct than theirs.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנִרְאִין דְּבָרָיו מִדִּבְרֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the views of steps 18 and 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אלעזר's view (הלל from the time of the sea) is preferred.

steps.title: First proof: they must have sung with the פסח and לולב
steps.stepSummary: Could it be that ישראל brought the קרבן פסח and took לולבים for hundreds of years before דוד without saying a song?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it possible that ישראל slaughtered their פסח offerings and took their לולבים and did not say a song?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי gives his first proof that הלל is older than דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Long before דוד, ישראל were already bringing the קרבן פסח and taking לולבים. It makes no sense that they did these happy מצוות with no song, so הלל must have existed already, from the time of the sea.

phrases.english: Is it possible that Israel slaughtered their Paschal lambs
and took their lulavim
and did not say a song?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question: obviously they did sing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶפְשָׁר יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁחֲטוּ אֶת פִּסְחֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the preference in step 20.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Logic: the מצוות of פסח and לולב were done for generations before דוד and surely came with song.

steps.title: Second proof: פסלו של מיכה
steps.stepSummary: Another reason: the idol of מיכה was still standing in דוד's time, so it cannot be that ישראל said הלל for the first time then.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: the idol of מיכה was standing, crying, and ישראל were saying הלל?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי gives a second proof that הלל did not start with דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idol of מיכה (from ספר שופטים) was still around in דוד's time. הלל mocks idols (כמוהם יהיו עושיהם), so it would be absurd for ישראל to first start saying it while an idol stood among them. So הלל must come from an earlier, pure time: the sea.

keyTerms.meaning: The idol of מיכה (ספר שופטים פרק י״ז)
Standing in tears (a polite way of saying 'laughing at them')

steps.confusionAlert: 'Crying' here really means the idol was laughing at ישראל. The גמרא uses the opposite word to avoid shaming ישראל (as the גאונים explain).

phrases.english: Another explanation:
Micah's idol was standing in tears,
phrases.notes: A euphemism: the idol was 'laughing' at them.

phrases.english: and Israel were saying Hallel?
phrases.notes: Rhetorical: that cannot be how it started.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: פִּסְלוֹ שֶׁל מִיכָה עוֹמֵד בִּבְכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate proof for the same preference.
steps.raayaObject: הלל did not first begin in דוד's time.
steps.raayaSupportSource: History: מיכה's idol was still standing in דוד's days.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוסי holds like his son: הלל was first said by משה and ישראל at the sea, with two proofs (פסח/לולב, and מיכה's idol).

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: דוד said the songs about himself
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא asks about all the songs דוד said in תהלים. רבי אליעזר says דוד said them about himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: all the songs and praises that דוד said in ספר תהלים — רבי אליעזר says: he said them about himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא with a new question: were דוד's songs about his own life or about the whole people? רבי אליעזר gives the first view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי אליעזר, every מזמור was about דוד's own personal experiences. Only later did the community take them on as their own prayers.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
All the songs and praises
that David said in the book of Psalms,
Rabbi Eliezer says:
He said them about himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כׇּל שִׁירוֹת וְתוּשְׁבָּחוֹת שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד בְּסֵפֶר תְּהִלִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a related topic about דוד's songs in תהלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All of דוד's songs were about himself.

steps.title: רבי יהושע: about the community
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע says דוד said all the songs about the community.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע says: he said them about the community.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the ברייתא: דוד wrote all his songs for the whole people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite of רבי אליעזר. Even songs that sound personal were really written with the community in mind.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says:
He said them about the community.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר: כְּנֶגֶד צִיבּוּר אֲמָרָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי אליעזר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All of דוד's songs were about the community.

steps.title: חכמים: some of each
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say some songs are about the community and some are about דוד himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים say: some of them are about the community, and some of them are about himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The third opinion takes a middle path: both kinds exist.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים do not choose one side. The next step tells us how to know which song is which.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
Some of them are about the community
and some of them are about himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: יֵשׁ מֵהֶן כְּנֶגֶד צִיבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A middle position between רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Some songs are personal, some are for the community.

steps.title: How to tell: singular or plural
steps.stepSummary: Songs written in the singular are about דוד himself; songs written in the plural are about the community.
steps.simpleTranslation: Those said in the singular are about himself; those said in the plural are about the community.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים explain their rule: look at the grammar of the song.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the מזמור says 'I' or 'me', it is דוד's own song. If it says 'we' or 'us', it was said for the whole people.

phrases.english: Those stated in the singular — are about himself;
those stated in the plural — are about the community.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאֲמוּרוֹת בִּלְשׁוֹן יָחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how to apply the חכמים's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Singular = personal; plural = communal.
steps.whatToRemember: Three views: רבי אליעזר (all personal), רבי יהושע (all communal), חכמים (depends on singular or plural wording).

steps.title: What נצוח, נגון and משכיל mean
steps.stepSummary: Songs with the words נצוח or נגון are about the future; a song called משכיל was said through a תורגמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'נצוח' and 'נגון' — about the time to come. 'משכיל' — through a תורגמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a list explaining what different opening words of a מזמור teach us.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A song opening with למנצח or בנגינות speaks about something that will happen in the future. A משכיל was taught in public: דוד spoke quietly and a תורגמן repeated it loudly for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: From 'למנצח', an opening word in some מזמורים
Spokesman who repeats a speaker's words loudly to a crowd

phrases.english: 'Nitzuach' and 'niggun' — refer to the future.
'Maskil' — was said through a disseminator.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״נִיצּוּחַ״ וְ״נִיגּוּן״ — לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues discussing features of ספר תהלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Opening words of a מזמור tell us its nature.

steps.title: לדוד מזמור vs. מזמור לדוד
steps.stepSummary: 'לדוד מזמור' means the שכינה rested on דוד first and then he sang; 'מזמור לדוד' means he sang first and then the שכינה rested on him.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'לדוד מזמור' teaches that the שכינה rested on him and afterwards he said a song. 'מזמור לדוד' teaches that he said a song and afterwards the שכינה rested on him.
steps.whatsHappening: The list ends by explaining how the order of the words 'לדוד' and 'מזמור' teaches the order of events.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When 'לדוד' (about דוד's state) comes first, the שכינה came first and inspired the song. When 'מזמור' (the song) comes first, the singing came first and brought the שכינה down onto him.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Of דוד, a song' — שכינה first, then song
'A song of דוד' — song first, then שכינה
The Divine Presence rested on him

steps.whatToRemember: The word order matters: whichever comes first, 'לדוד' (the שכינה) or 'מזמור' (the song), happened first.

phrases.english: 'Of David, a psalm' —
teaches that the Divine Presence rested upon him
and afterward he said the song.
'A psalm of David' —
teaches that he said the song
and afterward the Divine Presence rested upon him.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״לְדָוִד מִזְמוֹר״ — מְלַמֵּד שֶׁשָּׁרְתָה עָלָיו שְׁכִינָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the list of opening words in תהלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The order of 'לדוד' and 'מזמור' shows whether the שכינה or the song came first.

steps.title: The Divine Presence rests only through the joy of a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The שכינה does not rest on a person who is lazy, sad, laughing, light-headed or chatting idly. It rests only through שמחה של מצוה, as shown by אלישע and the musician.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches you that the שכינה does not rest on a person through laziness, sadness, laughter, light-headedness or empty talk. It rests only through the joy of a מצוה. As the פסוק says: 'Now bring me a musician. And when the musician played, the hand of ה׳ came upon him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a lesson from the previous step, where the שכינה could come to דוד through his singing. The lesson is that the שכינה comes only when a person is in a state of מצוה-joy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא lists five wrong moods: laziness, sadness, laughter, light-headedness and idle talk. Only one right mood brings the שכינה: שמחה של מצוה. The proof is that נבואה left אלישע after he became angry, and it returned only once music had restored his joy.

keyTerms.meaning: The joy that comes from doing a מצוה

steps.confusionAlert: שחוק (laughter) is on the 'wrong' list even though it looks happy. The point is that silly fun is not the same as the joy of a מצוה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle is the base for the next two steps, which extend it to teaching הלכה and to dreams.

phrases.english: To teach you that the Divine Presence does not rest
not from laziness
and not from sadness
and not from laughter
and not from light-headedness
and not from idle talk,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ דְּבַר שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה.
phrases.english: but rather from a matter of the joy of a מצוה.
As it says: 'And now bring me a musician,
phrases.notes: מלכים ב ג:טו, spoken by אלישע

phrases.english: and it was, as the musician played,
the hand of God came upon him.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לְלַמֶּדְךָ שֶׁאֵין הַשְּׁכִינָה שׁוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general lesson from step 28, where the שכינה could come to דוד through song.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The שכינה rests only through שמחה של מצוה, not through laziness, sadness, laughter, frivolity or idle talk.

steps.title: The same joy is needed for saying הלכה
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב: the same rule applies to a matter of הלכה. One should be joyful when teaching it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: the same is true for a matter of הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב extends the rule of מצוה-joy from נבואה to teaching הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as the שכינה needs a joyful setting, clear Torah teaching also comes through joy. This new extension is exactly what the גמרא will soon challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: And so too, the same applies

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
And so too for a matter of halacha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: וְכֵן לִדְבַר הֲלָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the joy principle of step 29 to teaching הלכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should approach a matter of הלכה with joy.

steps.title: The same joy brings a good dream
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן adds that the same is true for a good dream. One should go to sleep in a joyful state.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: the same is true for a good dream.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן adds another area where the joy rule applies: dreams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A good dream is a small kind of message from above, so it also depends on going to sleep in a happy mood. This is a second extension of the rule in step 29, next to רב's extension to הלכה.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
And so too for a good dream.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: וְכֵן לַחֲלוֹם טוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel extension of step 29, beside רב's extension in step 30.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Going to sleep in joy leads to a good dream.

steps.title: Challenge: a student's lips must drip with bitterness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that הלכה needs joy. רב himself said, through רב גידל, that a תלמיד חכם before his רבי must have lips 'dripping with bitterness', and he reads this from a פסוק in שיר השירים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? רב גידל said in the name of רב: any תלמיד חכם who sits before his teacher and whose lips do not drip with bitterness, those lips should be burned. As it says: 'His lips are lilies, dripping with flowing myrrh.' Do not read 'שושנים' (lilies) but 'ששונים' (who are learning). Do not read 'מור עובר' (flowing myrrh) but 'מר עובר' (flowing bitterness).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's statement from step 30. Torah learning is supposed to be joyful, yet רב himself demanded bitterness and fear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge sets רב against רב. In step 30 Torah learning should be joyful, but here the lips of those who study must be 'bitter' with awe of the teacher. The proof comes from rereading two words of the פסוק: שושנים becomes ששונים (those who learn), and מור becomes מר (bitter).

keyTerms.meaning: Dripping with bitterness, meaning awe and fear
Do not read it as... (a reading-based דרשה)

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תקרי' does not change the text of the פסוק. It is a דרשה that reads a second meaning into the same letters.

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But didn't Rav Giddel say that Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הַיּוֹשֵׁב לִפְנֵי רַבּוֹ
phrases.english: Any Torah scholar who sits before his teacher
and his lips are not dripping with bitterness, they should be burned,
as it says: 'His lips are lilies,
phrases.notes: שיר השירים ה:יג

phrases.english: dripping with flowing myrrh.'
Do not read 'lilies', but rather 'who are learning'.
Do not read 'flowing myrrh', but rather 'flowing bitterness'.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 30 with a conflicting teaching from the same רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's statement that הלכה should be approached with joy
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב also taught that one learning Torah before his רבי must be filled with bitterness and awe, which seems to be the opposite of joy.

steps.title: Joy is for the teacher, awe is for the student
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. The joy statement refers to the רבי who teaches, and the bitterness statement refers to the student sitting before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not a contradiction. This one refers to the teacher, and that one refers to the student.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by splitting the two statements between two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both statements of רב stay true. They simply apply to different roles. The teacher should open his הלכה with joy, while the student must sit before his teacher with awe and seriousness.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
This one... that one (splitting two cases)

steps.whatToRemember: The שכינה and Torah come through שמחה של מצוה. A רבי teaches with joy, but a student sits before his רבי with awe ('bitter lips').

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this refers to a teacher,
that refers to a student.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא בְּרַבָּה, הָא בְּתַלְמִידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of step 32.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the person's role (teacher versus student)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both statements seemed to apply to anyone learning Torah, so they contradicted each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The joy statement is about the teacher, and the bitterness statement is about the student.

steps.title: Second answer: joy before teaching, awe after starting
steps.stepSummary: Both statements, joy and bitterness, are about the teacher. Joy is before he begins teaching, and bitterness and awe are after he begins.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say: both statements are about the teacher, and there is no contradiction. The joy statement is before he begins teaching. The bitterness statement is after he has begun.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second way to settle the contradiction from step 32. This time it splits the two statements by time, not by person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 33 the split was teacher (joy) versus student (bitterness). Here both statements describe the same רבי at two different moments. He starts in a joyful mood, and once the real learning begins he becomes serious and full of awe.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say. This introduces another possible answer.
And it is not difficult. There is no real contradiction.

steps.confusionAlert: Here בְּרַבָּה means 'about the teacher'. It is not the name of the אמורא רבה, even though the next line tells a story about רבה.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
this and that are both about the teacher,
and it is not difficult:
this one (joy) is before he begins teaching,
phrases.notes: Joy belongs to the opening moment.

phrases.english: and that one (bitterness) is after he has begun.
phrases.notes: Serious awe belongs to the learning itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא בְּרַבָּה, וְלָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the same contradiction that step 33 resolved.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting by time (before teaching versus during teaching)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Joy and bitterness seemed to clash for the same person at the same time.
steps.terutzMaskana: The same teacher starts with joy and then teaches with serious awe.

steps.title: רבה's practice: a joke first, then serious learning
steps.stepSummary: רבה would tell a light joke to cheer the students. Then he sat in awe and began the lesson.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like רבה's practice. Before he began teaching the scholars, he would say something funny, and they would be cheered. In the end he sat in awe and began the lesson.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows a real-life example of the answer it just gave. רבה actually taught this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story fits the two-stage model. The joke opens hearts and gives the joy needed before teaching. The serious sitting in awe is the bitterness and fear that fit the learning itself.

keyTerms.meaning: The lesson, the הלכה being taught

steps.whatToRemember: A good teacher opens with warmth and joy, then teaches with seriousness and awe.
steps.whyThisMatters: This became a famous model for how to teach Torah: begin with something light to open the students' minds, then turn to serious learning.

phrases.english: Like this practice of Rabba:
before he began teaching the Sages,
he would say something humorous
and the Sages would be cheered;
and in the end he sat in awe
and began the lesson.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates and supports the answer given in step 34.
steps.raayaObject: The two-stage model: joy before teaching, awe during it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The practice of רבה with his students.

steps.title: A ברייתא asks: who first said הלל?
steps.stepSummary: A new topic begins. A ברייתא asks who first recited this הלל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: this הלל, who first said it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the joy discussion and returns to the question of who first said הלל, which was already raised in steps 13 and 17. This step sets up the question, and the opinions that answer it come in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects back to the הלל of the סדר. The question asks about the historical origin of הלל: on what occasion was it first sung?

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught. This introduces a ברייתא.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
This hallel, who said it?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַלֵּל זֶה מִי אֲמָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the joy discussion and returns to the question of who first said הלל, asked earlier in steps 13 and 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The first people to recite הלל, and the occasion.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: משה and Israel at the sea
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר says משה and Israel first said הלל at the sea. They said 'Not to us', and רוח הקודש answered 'For My sake'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: משה and Israel said it when they stood at the sea. They said, 'Not to us, ה׳, not to us.' רוח הקודש answered them, 'For My sake, for My sake I will do it.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first answer to the question. It places the origin of הלל at קריעת ים סוף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The people humbly say the salvation is not because of their merit, quoting a פסוק from הלל. רוח הקודש replies with a פסוק from ישעיה‎: ה׳ saves for the sake of His own Name. This same exchange is repeated for every opinion that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: Stood at the sea (קריעת ים סוף)
'Not to us', a פסוק in הלל (תהילים 115:1)
'For My sake I will do it' (ישעיה 48:11)

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
Moses and Israel said it
when they stood at the sea.

phrases.aramaic: הֵם אָמְרוּ: ״לֹא לָנוּ ה׳ לֹא לָנוּ״,
phrases.english: They said: 'Not to us, God, not to us,'
the Divine Spirit responded and said to them:
'For My sake, for My sake, will I do it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: מֹשֶׁה וְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲמָרוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the question in step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: משה and Israel at קריעת ים סוף.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: יהושע and Israel against the kings of כנען
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says יהושע and Israel first said הלל when the kings of כנען stood against them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: יהושע and Israel said it when the kings of כנען stood against them. They said 'Not to us', and רוח הקודש answered, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second, different answer. It moves the origin of הלל to the conquest of the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern stays the same: a moment of danger, then 'Not to us', then 'For My sake'. Only the historical event changes. 'וכו׳' is shorthand for the full answer of רוח הקודש from the previous step.

keyTerms.meaning: Joshua, who led the conquest of ארץ ישראל
Etc., meaning the same reply as before

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Joshua and Israel said it
when the kings of Canaan stood against them.
They said: 'Not to us,' and [the Divine Spirit] responded, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וְיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲמָרוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי אליעזר about the occasion.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: יהושע and Israel against the kings of כנען.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר המודעי: דבורה and ברק against סיסרא
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר המודעי says דבורה and ברק first said הלל when סיסרא attacked them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר המודעי says: דבורה and ברק said it when סיסרא stood against them. They said 'Not to us', and רוח הקודש answered them, 'For My sake, for My sake I will do it.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a third answer. It places the origin in the time of the שופטים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the full reply of רוח הקודש is written out again. The idea is unchanged: the people give all credit to ה׳, and ה׳ saves for His Name's sake.

keyTerms.meaning: Deborah the prophetess and Barak the general

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i says:
Deborah and Barak said it
when Sisera stood against them.
They said: 'Not to us,'
and the Divine Spirit responded and said to them:
'For My sake, for My sake, will I do it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הַמּוֹדָעִי אוֹמֵר: דְּבוֹרָה וּבָרָק אֲמָרוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further opinion on the same question.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה: חזקיה against סנחריב
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה says חזקיה and his followers first said הלל when סנחריב besieged them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר בן עזריה says: חזקיה and his company said it when סנחריב stood against them. They said 'Not to us', and רוח הקודש answered, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a fourth answer. It places the origin in the time of the kings of יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The event changes to the Assyrian siege of ירושלים, but the same exchange between the people and רוח הקודש repeats.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says:
Hezekiah and his company said it
when Sennacherib stood against them.
They said: 'Not to us,' and [the Divine Spirit] responded, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אוֹמֵר: חִזְקִיָּה וְסִייעָתוֹ אֲמָרוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further opinion on the same question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: חזקיה and his company against סנחריב.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: חנניה, מישאל and עזריה against נבוכדנצר
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says חנניה, מישאל and עזריה first said הלל when נבוכדנצר threatened them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: חנניה, מישאל and עזריה said it when the wicked נבוכדנצר stood against them. They said 'Not to us', and רוח הקודש answered, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a fifth answer. It moves the origin to גלות בבל and the fiery furnace.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the danger is to a few individuals, not a whole army or nation. They still said 'Not to us' and received the same reply.

keyTerms.meaning: The three who were thrown into the furnace (דניאל ג)
The wicked Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah said it
when the wicked Nebuchadnezzar stood against them.
They said: 'Not to us,' and [the Divine Spirit] responded, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: חֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה אֲמָרוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further opinion on the same question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: חנניה, מישאל and עזריה against נבוכדנצר.

steps.title: רבי יוסי הגלילי: מרדכי and אסתר against המן
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי הגלילי says מרדכי and אסתר first said הלל when המן threatened the Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי הגלילי says: מרדכי and אסתר said it when the wicked המן stood against them. They said 'Not to us', and רוח הקודש answered, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the sixth and latest answer. It places the origin in the Purim story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Together, the six opinions move forward through history, from the sea to Purim. Each one ties the first recitation of הלל to a great rescue.

keyTerms.meaning: Mordecai and Esther of the Purim story

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says:
Mordecai and Esther said it
when the wicked Haman stood against them.
They said: 'Not to us,' and [the Divine Spirit] responded, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי אוֹמֵר: מָרְדְּכַי וְאֶסְתֵּר אֲמָרוּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further opinion on the same question.

steps.title: The חכמים: the נביאים set הלל for every trouble and every redemption
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say הלל was not tied to one event. The נביאים instituted it for Israel to say at every major occasion and every trouble, and to say it when they are redeemed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים say: the נביאים among them set up for Israel to say it at every important occasion and for every trouble (may it not come upon Israel). And when they are redeemed, they say it over their redemption.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the final opinion in the ברייתא. It answers the question differently: הלל was a general institution of the נביאים, not a song from one event.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each earlier opinion named one historical moment. The חכמים make הלל a permanent practice for all times: whenever trouble comes and whenever salvation arrives, Israel says הלל. This explains why we keep saying it, including at the סדר.

keyTerms.meaning: And the Sages say. This introduces the majority view.
On every important occasion or season

steps.whatToRemember: Six תנאים tie the first הלל to six different rescues, from the sea to Purim. The חכמים say the נביאים set הלל for every trouble and every redemption, so it belongs to all generations.
steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'שלא תבא עליהם' ('may it not come upon them') is a short prayer added in the middle of the sentence. It does not mean the trouble did not happen.
steps.whyThisMatters: This view explains why הלל is said at every redemption, including the redemption from מצרים celebrated at the סדר.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
the Prophets among them instituted for Israel
that they should recite it
on every significant occasion
and for every trouble
may it not come upon Israel.
phrases.notes: A short prayer inserted in the sentence.

phrases.english: And when they are redeemed, they recite it over their redemption.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים: נְבִיאִים שֶׁבֵּינֵיהֶן תִּיקְּנוּ לָהֶם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the list of opinions with a general rule instead of one historical event.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The נביאים instituted הלל to be said for every trouble and at every redemption.

steps.title: רב חסדא: הללויה ends the chapter
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that a הללויה standing between two chapters belongs to the end of the earlier chapter.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: "הללויה" is the end of the chapter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It asks where the word הללויה belongs when it sits between two chapters of תהלים. רב חסדא says it closes the chapter before it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Several chapters of תהלים have a הללויה right at the border with the next chapter. רב חסדא reads it as the closing word of the earlier chapter, a final shout of praise.

keyTerms.meaning: Praise God. A word of praise found at the edges of many chapters of תהלים

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
"Halleluya" is the end of the chapter.
phrases.notes: The הללויה closes the earlier psalm.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: הַלְלוּיָהּ סוֹף פִּירְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the origins of הלל to a textual question: how the word הללויה is divided between chapters.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A border הללויה belongs to the end of the earlier chapter.

steps.title: רבה בר רב הונא: הללויה starts the next chapter
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב הונא disagrees and says the הללויה opens the following chapter.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא said: "הללויה" is the start of the chapter.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives the opposite view. The הללויה is the first word of the next chapter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word and its spot in the text are the same for both. The only question is which chapter it is attached to. For רבה בר רב הונא, הללויה is an opening call to praise, not a closing one.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna said:
"Halleluya" is the start of the chapter.
phrases.notes: The הללויה opens the next psalm.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אָמַר: הַלְלוּיָהּ רֵישׁ פִּירְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposing side of the מחלוקת begun by רב חסדא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A border הללויה belongs to the start of the next chapter.

steps.title: הללויה written in between shows uncertainty
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא testifies that in רב חנין בר רב's תהלים scrolls, הללויה was written in the middle between chapters. This shows רב חנין בר רב was unsure where it belonged.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: I saw the תהלים scrolls of the house of רב חנין בר רב, in which "הללויה" was written in the middle of the chapter. Apparently he was in doubt about it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא reports something he saw with his own eyes. A scribe wrote הללויה floating between two chapters, attached to neither one. The גמרא concludes that the owner was in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "In the middle" here means in the space between the chapters, not inside a chapter. Writing it that way avoided taking a side. So the גמרא infers that רב חנין בר רב had not decided between the two views.

keyTerms.meaning: He was in doubt about it

steps.confusionAlert: "באמצע פירקא" does not mean in the middle of a psalm's text. It means in the gap between the two psalms, belonging to neither.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
I saw the Tehillim scrolls
of the house of Rav Chanin bar Rav
in which "Halleluya" was written
in the middle of the chapter (i.e., between chapters).
Apparently, he was in doubt about it.
phrases.notes: The גמרא's inference from how the scroll was written.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: חֲזֵינָא לְהוּ לְתִילֵּי דְּבֵי רַב חָנִין בַּר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the מחלוקת of steps 44 and 45 was a real uncertainty, even affecting how scrolls were written.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב חנין בר רב's scrolls left הללויה unattached, which shows the question was undecided.

steps.title: Three places where all agree הללויה opens the section
steps.stepSummary: רב חנין בר רבא lists three places where everyone agrees the הללויה after a certain verse begins the next section.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנין בר רבא said: Everyone agrees about these. After "My mouth shall speak the praise of God, and all flesh shall bless His holy name forever and ever," the הללויה that follows is the start of the chapter. After "The wicked shall see and be angry, he shall gnash his teeth and melt away; the desire of the wicked shall perish," the הללויה that follows is the start of the chapter. And after "who stand in the house of God," the הללויה that follows is the start of the chapter.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חנין בר רבא narrows the מחלוקת. In three specific places, even רב חסדא agrees that the הללויה opens the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three places are תהלים 145:21 (then 146 opens with הללויה), 112:10 (then 113 opens with הללויה), and 135:2 (then verse 3 opens with הללויה). In these spots the earlier text has already closed fully, so the הללויה can only be an opening. This means the מחלוקת applies only to the other border cases.

phrases.english: Rav Chanin bar Rava said:
Everyone agrees
regarding "My mouth shall speak the praise of God
phrases.notes: תהלים 145:21

phrases.english: and all flesh shall bless
His holy name forever and ever (Halleluya)",
the Halleluya that follows it is the start of the chapter.
phrases.notes: תהלים 146 opens with הללויה.

phrases.english: "The wicked shall see and be angry
phrases.notes: תהלים 112:10

phrases.english: he shall gnash his teeth and melt away
the desire of the wicked shall perish",
the Halleluya that follows it is the start of the chapter.
phrases.notes: תהלים 113 opens with הללויה.

phrases.english: And "who stand in the house of God",
phrases.notes: תהלים 135:2

phrases.english: the Halleluya that follows it is the start of the chapter.
phrases.notes: תהלים 135:3 begins with הללויה.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָנִין בַּר רָבָא: הַכֹּל מוֹדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the מחלוקת by naming the cases where both sides agree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After 145:21, 112:10 and 135:2, the הללויה that follows opens the next section according to all opinions.

steps.title: The Bible experts add two more places
steps.stepSummary: The קראי, experts in the text of תנ"ך, add two more cases where the following הללויה is a chapter opening.
steps.simpleTranslation: The experts in verses add these too. After "He will drink from the brook on the way; therefore he will lift up his head," the הללויה that follows is the start of the chapter. After "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God; good understanding to all who do them," the הללויה that follows is the start of the chapter.
steps.whatsHappening: The list from step 47 grows. The קראי add two more places where the הללויה clearly opens the next chapter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two verses are תהלים 110:7 (then 111 opens with הללויה) and 111:10 (then 112 opens with הללויה). The list is the same kind as before. It shows more spots where the הללויה cannot be a closing word.

keyTerms.meaning: Experts in the text of the Bible

phrases.english: The experts in verses add these too:
"He will drink from the brook on the way
phrases.notes: תהלים 110:7

phrases.english: therefore he will lift up his head",
the Halleluya that follows it is the start of the chapter.
phrases.notes: תהלים 111 opens with הללויה.

phrases.english: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God
phrases.notes: תהלים 111:10

phrases.english: good understanding to all who do them",
the Halleluya that follows it is the start of the chapter.
phrases.notes: תהלים 112 opens with הללויה.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָרָאֵי מוֹסִיפִין אַף אֶת אֵלּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds two more cases to רב חנין בר רבא's list of agreed places.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After 110:7 and 111:10, the following הללויה also opens the next chapter.
steps.whatToRemember: The מחלוקת of רב חסדא and רבה בר רב הונא applies only to unclear border cases. In five listed places, everyone agrees the הללויה opens the next section.

steps.title: Suggesting the dispute matches an argument of תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the הללויה מחלוקת may match a disagreement among תנאים. It first quotes the version where בית שמאי stop at "אם הבנים שמחה" and בית הלל stop at "חלמיש למעינו מים".
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say it is like a dispute of תנאים. Until where does one say הלל? בית שמאי say: until "a joyful mother of children." בית הלל say: until "the flint into a fountain of water."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a comparison. It suggests that the אמוראים' argument about הללויה may already appear in a disagreement of תנאים. It begins by quoting the first source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This first source is our own משנה, with its familiar מחלוקת about how much הלל to say before the meal at the סדר. בית שמאי stop at the end of chapter 113. בית הלל stop at the end of chapter 114. This version ends at the closing words of each chapter. A ברייתא, quoted next, will word the stopping points differently.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say this matches a dispute of תנאים

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute of Tannaim:
Until where does one say (Hallel)?
Beit Shammai say:

steps.title: A ברייתא uses different stopping points
steps.stepSummary: Unlike the משנה quoted in step 49, a ברייתא records the same dispute with different wording. בית שמאי say until "בצאת ישראל ממצרים" and בית הלל say until "לא לנו ה' לא לנו".
steps.simpleTranslation: And another ברייתא taught: Until where does one say הלל? בית שמאי say: until "When Israel went out of Egypt." And בית הלל say: until "Not to us, God, not to us."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes setting up its comparison by quoting the second version. The two versions name different words as the stopping point, and the גמרא will next explain how this links to the הללויה question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version names the opening words of the next chapter (114:1 and 115:1) instead of the closing words of the current one. The gap between the two versions covers exactly the border area where the הללויה sits after "אם הבנים שמחה". So the two versions seem to treat that הללויה differently: one as an ending, the other as an opening. That matches רב חסדא versus רבה בר רב הונא.
